newsitem.title: INDIA: India quickens chase for foreign investor billions.
newsitem.headline: India quickens chase for foreign investor billions.

text.p: India is speeding up the chase to lure the billions of dollars required to keep its high growth rate on track, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said on Tuesday.
Deve Gowda, speaking at the start of a two-day "Destination India" investment conference, said the country required $10 billion a year in foreign direct investment -- five times last year's total.
These amounts are needed to help put India in shape to cope with the social needs of a population now estimated at around 950 million. It is expected to hit one billion by the year 2000.
"I would like to see this great country move into a vibrant economy, on a path of significant progress. I would like to see that no person is deprived of basic necessities," Deve Gowda said.
"The commitment is to achieve GDP growth of 10 percent (annually) over the next 10 years and 12 percent growth in industry production," he told an audience of businessmen, bankers and diplomats.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by seven percent in fiscal year ended March 31, 1996. It was forecast to slow to 6.5 percent growth this fiscal year.
Deve Gowda sought to soothe concerns over a public sector borrowing requirement of over 10 percent of GDP and interest repayments sapping the government of nearly half its revenues.
"This has to be achieved with a low fiscal deficit and low inflation," he said.
The government has to pass its 1996/97 budget before the parliamentary session ends on Friday.
Deve Gowda, who has led the country since June, has vowed to continue the economic liberalisation started in 1991. Since then, the country has attracted $5 billion in foreign direct investment.
Investors have been cautious of Deve Gowda's loose-knit and left-leaning coalition, whose policies need to strike a balance between its centrist, socialist, communist and farming parties.
Deve Gowda said India was striving to improve the investor environment.
"Further refinements are underway to make it investor friendly," he said.
Industry Minister Murasoli Maran said he planned to widen the range of industries eligible for automatic approval for foreign investment.
Maran said in the past two months, 350 investment proposals totalling nearly four billion dollars had been approved.
One problem was that actual capital inflow from approved FDI was only 23 percent, Maran said, and substantial inflows were needed to overhaul the country's creaking infrastructure.
The government's Foreign Investment Promotion Board soon plans to tap into the Internet to boost the marketing of India's investment opportunities.
The proposed changes announced by Maran included an increase in the ceiling on foreign shareholdings in Indian companies for some high priority investment projects from the current 51 percent limit.

The Financial Express daily said on Tuesday that the government was considering raising the limit of foreign investments in such projects to 74 percent. Government officials were not immediately available for confirmation.
